newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German steel merger to cost 8,000 jobs.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German steel merger to cost 8,000 jobs.

text.p: A merger of the steel divisions of German industry giants Krupp and Thyssen would cost 8,000 jobs but both companies on Wednesday promised striking workers that they would not impose any forced layoffs.

Thyssen AG said it would announce the details of the tie-up at a news conference on Thursday afternoon after it reached a compromise which averted a hostile takeover bid launched by Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp last week.

"Workforce reductions will definitely be carried out with social compensation," Hans-Wilhelm Grasshoff, chairman of steel unit Krupp Hoesch Stahl, said in a statement. "We rule out any forced layoffs under this steel plan."

Ekkehard Schulz, chairman of Thyssen Stahl AG, which will take a 60 percent stake in and industrial control of the new company, also said he did not plan compulsory redundancies and added that the brunt of the job cuts would hit Krupp.

"We will not sign the merger contract if one thing is not guaranteed by Krupp Hoesch by tonight," Schulz said, seeking to assure an angry workforce that has waged work stoppages and protests for a week throughout the Ruhr Valley.

"The costs that arise by ruling out forced layoffs must not be borne by the new company or by Thyssen," he said, a clear indication that Thyssen would seek to make Krupp pay for its unwanted takeover bid.
Half of the planned job reductions have already been agreed in areas where the two firms already cooperate. The additional 4,000 job cuts would largely hit Krupp Hoesch's Dortmund steel works.

The steel merger would take four years to complete and create a producer with an annual capacity of 15 million tonnes of crude steel, putting it third in Europe behind British Steel and France's Usinor-Sacilor.
It would become Europe's biggest maker of flat steel products, whose key customers are Europe's car makers.

The new company will have a workforce of around 18,000, compared with a combined total of 26,000 now. It will transform Thyssen's Duisburg steel works into one of the world's biggest and most modern integrated mills, while Krupp Hoesch becomes more of an extended workbench for the new firm.

Wolfgang Clement, Economics Minister in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia -- where both Krupp and Thyssen are based -- said he expected a memorandum of understanding on the merger to be signed later on Wednesday.

Clement, who intervened to stave off Krupp's 13.6 billion mark ($8.1 billion) cash bid for Thyssen, told reporters the two companies would invest up to one billion marks in Krupp's Dortmund steel works, countering fears that it might be closed down.
But Krupp will face the brunt of job losses in Dortmund, where 3,600 jobs out of a workforce of 5,700 will have to go.
He said Krupp and Thyssen had pledged to create around 1,300 jobs in Dortmund in other areas to limit the total number of jobs that would be lost in the city.
The investment would transform Dortmund from a steel-producing plant to a processing plant with new, modern galvanising, joining and cold-rolling facilities.

The two companies' steelworks remained at a standstill on Wednesday after unions vowed to fight the creation of the joint venture. Workers threatened to strike for as long as it takes the two companies to hammer out details of the merger.
"If the companies need four weeks, then so do we," Juergen Hafner, works council chairman at the Krupp Hoesch Stahl plant, said late on Tuesday after being briefed by Krupp management.
Harald Schartau, head of the North Rhine-Westphalia unit of powerful steel and engineering union IG Metall, said the union would provide "massive resistance" against the job cuts.
Thyssen Stahl's Schulz told around 5,000 steel workers in Duisburg that job cuts would be made through offering early retirement and natural wastage over a period of four years.
"In the past we have always achieved workforce reductions with socially-acceptable methods. And that is the way we want to keep it in the future," he said.
-- Bonn Newsroom, 49 228 26097 150 ($ = 1.685 German Marks)
